claims.text: The initial material is a melt of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Under conventional cooling, Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 forms multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Conventionally quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a sequence of crystallization exotherms during reheating.
Applying approximately 1 GPa isostatic pressure during the liquid-to-solid transition will modify the alloy's free-energy landscape.
Approximately 1 GPa pressure will elevate the nucleation barrier for crystalline phases.
High pressure increases the Gibbs free energy required to nucleate crystalline phases in this alloy.
The elevated nucleation barrier will suppress the formation and growth of primary non-eutectic phases during cooling.
Suppressing primary crystallization will stabilize a larger amorphous fraction after solidification.
High-pressure quenching will produce a higher amorphous phase fraction than quenching at atmospheric pressure.
The increased amorphous stabilization will delay crystallization onset during subsequent reheating.
High-pressure-quenched samples will show a reduced crystallization exotherm or an exotherm shifted to higher temperature in DSC.
High-pressure quenching will reduce the alloy's multistep crystallization sequence.
The intervention will improve thermal stability during reheating.
The intervention will be effective at cooling rates of at least 10^5 K/s.
The intervention will also be effective at cooling rates of approximately 10^3 K/s.
The exact pressure threshold and pressure-dependent phase behavior remain undetermined.
